newsitem.title: GERMANY: U.N. swears in sea tribunal judges in Hamburg.
newsitem.headline: U.N. swears in sea tribunal judges in Hamburg.

text.p: The United Nations swore in 21 judges for a world maritime tribunal in the German port of Hamburg on Friday, launching a unique court with jurisdiction over three-quarters of the earth.

U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali presided over the ceremony in Hamburg's city hall, crowning a quarter of a century of efforts to deal better with oil spills, fishing rights, deep-sea mining and other sea-faring problems.

"With the establishment of this tribunal, we enter a new era of maritime justice," he said at the swearing-in. "Because maritime disputes can be a source of conflict between countries, the tribunal has an important role to play."

Boutros-Ghali said the Hamburg-based tribunal was "dedicated to resolve disputes of the seas and oceans and on the seafloor -- a jurisdiction which includes 75 percent of the surface of our blue planet."
German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said the long years of preparation for the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea had produced a constitution for the world's oceans.

"It regulates all possible uses of the sea like trade and shipping, rights for overflights and cable-laying, sea research and environmental protection, conserving fish stocks and the economic use of off-shore and deep sea seabeds," he said.
The sea law convention, which was opened for signature in 1982 and entered into force 12 years later, binds all participating states to settle disputes by peaceful means.
Where no settlement can be reached, the international tribunal will be the central forum for dealing with disputes.

The judges come from 21 sea-faring nations from all over the world -- five each from Africa and Asia, four from Latin America and the Caribbean, four from Western Europe and three from Eastern Europe.
A total of 104 countries has signed the convention.
Boutros-Ghali said the tribunal would have the right to take prompt measures against pollution and order the release of arrested vessels on the deposit of a bond.
The choice of Hamburg, with a long tradition of shipping and trade, is a sign of Germany's increasing role within the U.N.
It is the second U.N. headquarters to be established in Germany, which is campaigning for a permanent seat on the world body's security council.
Hamburg Mayor Henning Voscherau said his city already had a long tradition of maritime law, which was a key focus of research at the local university and among local law firms.
